concepts.name: Function of two variables
concepts.statement: A function of two variables z = f(x, y) maps each ordered pair (x, y) in a subset D of the real plane ℝ² to a unique real number z. The set D is called the domain of the function, and the range of f is the set of all real numbers z that has at least one ordered pair (x, y) ∈ D such that f(x, y) = z.

concepts.name: Graph of a function of two variables
terms: graph of a function of two variables
concepts.statement: The graph of a function z = f(x, y) of two variables is the set of ordered triples (x, y, z) that satisfies the equation z = f(x, y), plotted in three-dimensional Cartesian space; it is called a surface. A point with positive z lies above the xy-plane and one with negative z below it.

concepts.name: Level curve of a function of two variables
terms: level curve of a function of two variables
concepts.statement: Given a function f(x, y) and a number c in the range of f, a level curve of a function of two variables for the value c is the set of points satisfying the equation f(x, y) = c, completely analogous to a contour line on a topographical map.

concepts.name: Contour map
concepts.statement: A contour map is a graph of the various level curves of a given function f(x, y); where the level curves are obtained for equally spaced values, curves close together mark a steep surface.

concepts.name: Vertical trace
concepts.statement: Consider a function z = f(x, y) with domain D ⊆ ℝ². A vertical trace of the function is either the set of points that solves the equation f(a, y) = z for a given constant x = a, or f(x, b) = z for a given constant y = b; it is graphed in a plane parallel to the yz- or xz-plane.

concepts.name: Functions of more than two variables
concepts.statement: A function of three variables f(x, y, z) maps each point in space to a fourth quantity, such as temperature or wind speed, and a function g(x, y, t) may map a point of the plane to a quantity at a time t. The domain of such a function is found as for one or two variables, from the restrictions that keep its value defined and real.

concepts.name: Level surface of a function of three variables
terms: level surface of a function of three variables
concepts.statement: Given a function f(x, y, z) and a number c in the range of f, a level surface of a function of three variables is the set of points satisfying the equation f(x, y, z) = c.

concepts.name: δ disk
concepts.statement: A δ disk centered at a point (a, b) ∈ ℝ² is the open disk of radius δ centered at (a, b), the set {(x, y) ∈ ℝ² | (x − a)² + (y − b)² < δ²}; it extends the idea of an open interval a − δ < x < a + δ to two variables.

concepts.name: Limit of a function of two variables
concepts.statement: The limit of f(x, y) as (x, y) approaches (a, b) is L, written lim_{(x,y)→(a,b)} f(x, y) = L, if for each ε > 0 there exists a small enough δ > 0 such that for all points (x, y) in a δ disk around (a, b), except possibly for (a, b) itself, the value of f(x, y) is no more than ε away from L: |f(x, y) − L| < ε whenever 0 < √((x − a)² + (y − b)²) < δ.

concepts.name: Limit laws for functions of two variables
concepts.statement: Let f(x, y) and g(x, y) be defined for all (x, y) ≠ (a, b) in a neighborhood around (a, b), with lim f(x, y) = L and lim g(x, y) = M as (x, y) → (a, b), and let c be a constant. Then the limit of a constant is the constant, the limits of x and y are a and b, and the limits of a sum, difference, constant multiple, product, quotient (M ≠ 0), power and root are L + M, L − M, cL, LM, L/M, Lⁿ and ⁿ√L.

concepts.name: A limit must not depend on the path
concepts.statement: Since (a, b) can be approached from an infinite number of directions, the limit of a function of two variables must be the same along every path toward (a, b); if the values of f approach different numbers along two paths, the limit fails to exist.

concepts.name: Interior point
concepts.statement: Let S be a subset of ℝ². A point P₀ is called an interior point of S if there is a δ disk centered around P₀ contained completely in S.

concepts.name: Boundary point
concepts.statement: Let S be a subset of ℝ². A point P₀ is called a boundary point of S if every δ disk centered around P₀ contains points both inside and outside S.

concepts.name: Open set
concepts.statement: A subset S of ℝ² is called an open set if every point of S is an interior point; a δ disk is an example.

concepts.name: Closed set
concepts.statement: A subset S of ℝ² is called a closed set if it contains all its boundary points; a δ disk with its boundary circle included is an example, and a set that contains some but not all of its boundary points is neither open nor closed.

concepts.name: Connected set
concepts.statement: An open set S is a connected set if it cannot be represented as the union of two or more disjoint, nonempty open subsets.

concepts.name: Region
concepts.statement: A set S in ℝ² is a region if it is open, connected and nonempty.

concepts.name: Limit of a function at a boundary point
concepts.statement: Let f be a function of two variables and suppose (a, b) is on the boundary of its domain. The limit of f(x, y) as (x, y) approaches (a, b) is L if for any ε > 0 there exists a δ > 0 such that, for every point (x, y) inside the domain of f and within distance δ of (a, b), |f(x, y) − L| < ε; only the points inside both the δ disk and the domain count.

concepts.name: Continuity of a function of two variables
concepts.statement: A function f(x, y) is continuous at a point (a, b) in its domain if f(a, b) exists, lim_{(x,y)→(a,b)} f(x, y) exists, and lim_{(x,y)→(a,b)} f(x, y) = f(a, b); in terms of ε and δ, |f(x, y) − f(a, b)| < ε whenever √((x − a)² + (y − b)²) < δ.

concepts.name: The sum of continuous functions is continuous
concepts.statement: If f(x, y) is continuous at (x₀, y₀) and g(x, y) is continuous at (x₀, y₀), then f(x, y) + g(x, y) is continuous at (x₀, y₀).

concepts.name: The product of continuous functions is continuous
concepts.statement: If g(x) is continuous at x₀ and h(y) is continuous at y₀, then f(x, y) = g(x)h(y) is continuous at (x₀, y₀).

concepts.name: The composition of continuous functions is continuous
concepts.statement: Let g be a function of two variables from a domain D ⊆ ℝ² to a range R ⊆ ℝ, continuous at (x₀, y₀) ∈ D, and let z₀ = g(x₀, y₀). If f maps ℝ to ℝ and is continuous at z₀, then f ∘ g is continuous at (x₀, y₀).

concepts.name: δ ball
concepts.statement: A δ ball in three dimensions about (x₀, y₀, z₀) consists of all points in ℝ³ lying at a distance of less than δ from it, {(x, y, z) ∈ ℝ³ | √((x − x₀)² + (y − y₀)² + (z − z₀)²) < δ}; a δ ball in more dimensions adds a term under the radical for each. The limit and continuity of a function of three or more variables are defined with δ balls as for two variables with δ disks.

concepts.name: Partial derivative
concepts.statement: Let f(x, y) be a function of two variables. The partial derivative of f with respect to x, written ∂f/∂x or f_x, is ∂f/∂x = lim_{h→0} [f(x + h, y) − f(x, y)]/h, and the partial derivative with respect to y, ∂f/∂y or f_y, is lim_{k→0} [f(x, y + k) − f(x, y)]/k: a derivative of a function of more than one independent variable in which all the variables but one are held constant.

concepts.name: Calculating partial derivatives
concepts.statement: To calculate a partial derivative, treat all independent variables other than the one with respect to which we are differentiating as constants, then differentiate as with a function of a single variable; all the differentiation rules apply.

concepts.name: A partial derivative as a slope
concepts.statement: ∂f/∂x represents the slope of the tangent line passing through the point (x, y, f(x, y)) parallel to the x-axis, the limit of the slopes of secant lines through (x, y, f(x, y)) and (x + h, y, f(x + h, y)), and ∂f/∂y the slope of the tangent line through that point parallel to the y-axis; each is a rate of change of f as we travel parallel to an axis.

concepts.name: Partial derivatives of a function of three variables
concepts.statement: Let f(x, y, z) be a function of three variables. Its partial derivatives with respect to x, y and z are ∂f/∂x = lim_{h→0} [f(x + h, y, z) − f(x, y, z)]/h, ∂f/∂y = lim_{k→0} [f(x, y + k, z) − f(x, y, z)]/k and ∂f/∂z = lim_{m→0} [f(x, y, z + m) − f(x, y, z)]/m, written also f_x, f_y and f_z.

concepts.name: Higher-order partial derivatives
concepts.statement: Each partial derivative of f(x, y) is itself a function of two variables, and its partial derivatives are the second-order partial derivatives ∂²f/∂x², ∂²f/∂x∂y, ∂²f/∂y∂x and ∂²f/∂y² (f_xx, f_yx, f_xy and f_yy), then third-order and so on: second-order or higher partial derivatives, regardless of whether they are mixed.

forms.latex: \frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial x^{2}}=\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left[\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\right],\;\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial x\partial y}=\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left[\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\right],\;\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial y\partial x}=\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left[\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\right],\;\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial y^{2}}=\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left[\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\right]

concepts.name: Mixed partial derivatives
concepts.statement: Higher-order partial derivatives calculated with respect to different variables, such as f_xy and f_yx, are called mixed partial derivatives: at least two of the differentiations are with respect to different variables.

concepts.name: Equality of mixed partial derivatives (Clairaut's theorem)
concepts.statement: Suppose that f(x, y) is defined on an open disk D that contains the point (a, b). If the functions f_xy and f_yx are continuous on D, then f_xy = f_yx: as long as the mixed second-order derivatives are continuous, the order of differentiation does not matter, and the result extends to higher-order derivatives.

concepts.name: Partial differential equation
concepts.statement: A partial differential equation is an equation that involves an unknown function of more than one independent variable and one or more of its partial derivatives.

concepts.name: Heat equation
concepts.statement: The heat equation in two dimensions is u_t = c²(u_xx + u_yy), where the unknown function u(x, y, t) has the spatial variables x and y and the time t and c is a constant; in one dimension it is u_t = c²u_xx, where c² is the thermal diffusivity of the material, and in radial coordinates ∂T/∂t = K[∂²T/∂r² + (2/r) ∂T/∂r].

concepts.name: Wave equation
concepts.statement: The wave equation in two dimensions is u_tt = c²(u_xx + u_yy), where the unknown function u(x, y, t) has the spatial variables x and y and the time t and c is an arbitrary constant.

concepts.name: Laplace's equation
concepts.statement: Laplace's equation in two dimensions is u_xx + u_yy = 0, where the unknown function u has the two independent variables x and y.

concepts.name: A solution of the one-dimensional heat equation
concepts.statement: A solution of u_t = c²u_xx can be written u_m(x, t) = e^{−π²m²c²t} sin(mπx), where m is any positive integer; with m = 1 and initial temperature sin πx over a wire of length 1, the wire cools as time progresses.

concepts.name: Tangent plane
concepts.statement: Let P₀ be a point on a surface S and let C be any curve passing through P₀ and lying entirely in S. If the tangent lines to all such curves C at P₀ lie in the same plane, this plane is the tangent plane to S at P₀. For a surface defined by a differentiable function z = f(x, y), the tangent plane at (x₀, y₀) is z = f(x₀, y₀) + f_x(x₀, y₀)(x − x₀) + f_y(x₀, y₀)(y − y₀), with normal vector f_x(x₀, y₀) i + f_y(x₀, y₀) j − k.

concepts.name: Linear approximation of a function of two variables
concepts.statement: Given a function z = f(x, y) with continuous partial derivatives that exist at the point (x₀, y₀), the linear approximation of f at (x₀, y₀) is L(x, y) = f(x₀, y₀) + f_x(x₀, y₀)(x − x₀) + f_y(x₀, y₀)(y − y₀), the tangent plane to z = f(x, y) at that point; for (x, y) reasonably close to (x₀, y₀) it yields a value reasonably close to f(x, y).

concepts.name: Differentiability of a function of two variables
concepts.statement: A function f(x, y) is differentiable at a point P(x₀, y₀) if, for all points (x, y) in a δ disk around P, f(x, y) = f(x₀, y₀) + f_x(x₀, y₀)(x − x₀) + f_y(x₀, y₀)(y − y₀) + E(x, y), where the error term E satisfies lim E(x, y)/√((x − x₀)² + (y − y₀)²) = 0 as (x, y) → (x₀, y₀): the graph is smooth there, close to its tangent plane near P.

concepts.name: Differentiability implies continuity for functions of two variables
concepts.statement: Let z = f(x, y) be a function of two variables with (x₀, y₀) in its domain. If f(x, y) is differentiable at (x₀, y₀), then f(x, y) is continuous at (x₀, y₀); a function continuous at a point need not be differentiable there.

concepts.name: Continuity of first partials implies differentiability
concepts.statement: Let z = f(x, y) be a function of two variables with (x₀, y₀) in its domain. If f(x, y), f_x(x, y) and f_y(x, y) all exist in a neighborhood of (x₀, y₀) and are continuous at (x₀, y₀), then f(x, y) is differentiable there.

concepts.name: Total differential
concepts.statement: Let z = f(x, y) be differentiable at (x₀, y₀), with differentials dx = Δx and dy = Δy. The differential dz, also called the total differential of z = f(x, y) at (x₀, y₀), is dz = f_x(x₀, y₀) dx + f_y(x₀, y₀) dy; it approximates the change Δz = f(x₀ + Δx, y₀ + Δy) − f(x₀, y₀), so f(x + Δx, y + Δy) ≈ f(x, y) + f_x(x₀, y₀)Δx + f_y(x₀, y₀)Δy, and estimates the propagation of a measurement error.

concepts.name: Differentiability of a function of three variables
concepts.statement: A function f(x, y, z) is differentiable at P(x₀, y₀, z₀) if for all points in a δ ball around P, f(x, y, z) = f(x₀, y₀, z₀) + f_x(x₀, y₀, z₀)(x − x₀) + f_y(x₀, y₀, z₀)(y − y₀) + f_z(x₀, y₀, z₀)(z − z₀) + E(x, y, z), where E(x, y, z)/√((x − x₀)² + (y − y₀)² + (z − z₀)²) → 0; it is then continuous there, and continuity of the first partial derivatives guarantees it.

concepts.name: Chain rule for one independent variable
concepts.statement: Suppose that x = g(t) and y = h(t) are differentiable functions of t and z = f(x, y) is a differentiable function of x and y. Then z = f(x(t), y(t)) is a differentiable function of t and dz/dt = (∂z/∂x)(dx/dt) + (∂z/∂y)(dy/dt), where the ordinary derivatives are evaluated at t and the partial derivatives at (x, y).

concepts.name: Intermediate variable
concepts.statement: Given a composition of functions such as f(x(t), y(t)), the intermediate variables are x and y: they are independent variables for the function f but dependent variables for the variable t.

concepts.name: Tree diagram
concepts.statement: A tree diagram for the chain rule starts at the dependent variable, branches once for each independent variable of the function and again for each variable those depend on, and labels each branch with its derivative; following the branches that end at one variable and adding the products along them gives the chain rule's formula for the derivative with respect to it.

concepts.name: Chain rule for two independent variables
concepts.statement: Suppose x = g(u, v) and y = h(u, v) are differentiable functions of u and v, and z = f(x, y) is a differentiable function of x and y. Then z = f(g(u, v), h(u, v)) is a differentiable function of u and v, and ∂z/∂u = (∂z/∂x)(∂x/∂u) + (∂z/∂y)(∂y/∂u), ∂z/∂v = (∂z/∂x)(∂x/∂v) + (∂z/∂y)(∂y/∂v).

forms.latex: \frac{\partial z}{\partial u}=\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\frac{\partial x}{\partial u}+\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}\frac{\partial y}{\partial u}
\frac{\partial z}{\partial v}=\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\frac{\partial x}{\partial v}+\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}\frac{\partial y}{\partial v}

concepts.name: Generalized chain rule
concepts.statement: Let w = f(x₁, x₂, …, x_m) be a differentiable function of m independent variables, and for each i let x_i = x_i(t₁, t₂, …, t_n) be a differentiable function of n independent variables. Then ∂w/∂t_j = (∂w/∂x₁)(∂x₁/∂t_j) + (∂w/∂x₂)(∂x₂/∂t_j) + ⋯ + (∂w/∂x_m)(∂x_m/∂t_j) for any j: the chain rule extended to functions of more than one independent variable.

forms.latex: \frac{\partial w}{\partial t_{j}}=\frac{\partial w}{\partial x_{1}}\frac{\partial x_{1}}{\partial t_{j}}+\frac{\partial w}{\partial x_{2}}\frac{\partial x_{2}}{\partial t_{j}}+\cdots +\frac{\partial w}{\partial x_{m}}\frac{\partial x_{m}}{\partial t_{j}}

concepts.name: Implicit differentiation of a function of two or more variables
concepts.statement: If the equation f(x, y) = 0 defines y implicitly as a function y = g(x) of x, then dy/dx = −(∂f/∂x)/(∂f/∂y), provided f_y(x, y) ≠ 0; if f(x, y, z) = 0 defines z implicitly as a differentiable function of x and y, then ∂z/∂x = −(∂f/∂x)/(∂f/∂z) and ∂z/∂y = −(∂f/∂y)/(∂f/∂z) as long as f_z(x, y, z) ≠ 0. It follows from the chain rule for two independent variables.

forms.latex: \frac{\partial z}{\partial x}=-\frac{\partial f/\partial x}{\partial f/\partial z}\;\text{and}\;\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}=-\frac{\partial f/\partial y}{\partial f/\partial z}

concepts.name: Directional derivative
concepts.statement: Suppose z = f(x, y) is a function of two variables with domain D, let (a, b) ∈ D and u = cos θ i + sin θ j. The directional derivative of f in the direction of u is D_u f(a, b) = lim_{h→0} [f(a + h cos θ, b + h sin θ) − f(a, b)]/h, provided the limit exists: the slope of the tangent line to the surface in the direction of u.

concepts.name: Directional derivative of a function of two variables
concepts.statement: Let z = f(x, y) be differentiable with f_x and f_y existing. Then the directional derivative of f in the direction of u = cos θ i + sin θ j is D_u f(x, y) = f_x(x, y) cos θ + f_y(x, y) sin θ, the dot product ∇f(x, y) · u.

concepts.name: Gradient
concepts.statement: Let z = f(x, y) be a function of x and y such that f_x and f_y exist. The vector ∇f(x, y) = f_x(x, y) i + f_y(x, y) j is called the gradient of f, read "del f" and also written "grad f"; for a nonunit direction vector, dividing by its norm gives the u of the directional derivative.

concepts.name: Properties of the gradient
concepts.statement: Suppose z = f(x, y) is differentiable at (x₀, y₀). If ∇f(x₀, y₀) = 0, then D_u f(x₀, y₀) = 0 for any unit vector u. If ∇f(x₀, y₀) ≠ 0, then D_u f(x₀, y₀) = ‖∇f(x₀, y₀)‖ cos φ is maximized when u points in the same direction as ∇f(x₀, y₀), with maximum value ‖∇f(x₀, y₀)‖, the rate of greatest ascent, and minimized when u points in the opposite direction, with minimum value −‖∇f(x₀, y₀)‖.

concepts.name: Gradient is normal to the level curve
concepts.statement: Suppose z = f(x, y) has continuous first-order partial derivatives in an open disk centered at (x₀, y₀). If ∇f(x₀, y₀) ≠ 0, then ∇f(x₀, y₀) is normal to the level curve of f at (x₀, y₀), since ∇f · ⟨x′(t), y′(t)⟩ = 0 along the level curve; reversing its components and multiplying one by −1 gives a tangent vector.

concepts.name: Gradient of a function of three variables
concepts.statement: Let w = f(x, y, z) be a function of three variables such that f_x, f_y and f_z exist. The vector ∇f(x, y, z) = f_x(x, y, z) i + f_y(x, y, z) j + f_z(x, y, z) k is called the gradient of f, also written grad f(x, y, z).

concepts.name: Directional derivative of a function of three variables
concepts.statement: Suppose w = f(x, y, z) has domain D, (x₀, y₀, z₀) ∈ D, and u = cos α i + cos β j + cos γ k is a unit vector whose components are the directional cosines. The directional derivative of f in the direction of u is D_u f(x₀, y₀, z₀) = lim_{t→0} [f(x₀ + t cos α, y₀ + t cos β, z₀ + t cos γ) − f(x₀, y₀, z₀)]/t, provided the limit exists; for a differentiable f it equals ∇f(x, y, z) · u = f_x cos α + f_y cos β + f_z cos γ.

concepts.name: Critical point of a function of two variables
terms: critical point of a function of two variables
concepts.statement: Let z = f(x, y) be defined on an open set containing (x₀, y₀). The point (x₀, y₀) is a critical point of f if f_x(x₀, y₀) = f_y(x₀, y₀) = 0, or if either f_x(x₀, y₀) or f_y(x₀, y₀) does not exist.

concepts.name: Local and global extrema of a function of two variables
concepts.statement: Let z = f(x, y) be defined and continuous on an open set containing (x₀, y₀). Then f has a local maximum at (x₀, y₀) if f(x₀, y₀) ≥ f(x, y) for all points within some disk centered at (x₀, y₀), and a local minimum if f(x₀, y₀) ≤ f(x, y) there; where the inequality holds for every point of the domain, the maximum or minimum is global (absolute). Either local value is a local extremum.

concepts.name: Fermat's theorem for functions of two variables
concepts.statement: Let z = f(x, y) be defined and continuous on an open set containing (x₀, y₀), and suppose f_x and f_y each exist at (x₀, y₀). If f has a local extremum at (x₀, y₀), then (x₀, y₀) is a critical point of f.

concepts.name: Saddle point
concepts.statement: Given z = f(x, y), the point (x₀, y₀, f(x₀, y₀)) is a saddle point if both f_x(x₀, y₀) = 0 and f_y(x₀, y₀) = 0 but f does not have a local extremum at (x₀, y₀); at the origin of z = x² − y² the surface is a maximum along one trace and a minimum along another.

concepts.name: Discriminant
concepts.statement: The discriminant of f(x, y) at a point (x₀, y₀) where f_x = f_y = 0 is D = f_xx(x₀, y₀) f_yy(x₀, y₀) − (f_xy(x₀, y₀))², which replaces f″(x₀) in the second derivative test.

concepts.name: Second derivative test for functions of two variables
concepts.statement: Let z = f(x, y) have continuous first- and second-order partial derivatives on some disk containing (x₀, y₀), with f_x(x₀, y₀) = f_y(x₀, y₀) = 0, and D its discriminant there. If D > 0 and f_xx(x₀, y₀) > 0, f has a local minimum at (x₀, y₀); if D > 0 and f_xx(x₀, y₀) < 0, a local maximum; if D < 0, a saddle point; if D = 0, the test is inconclusive.

concepts.name: Using the second derivative test for functions of two variables
concepts.statement: Determine the critical points (x₀, y₀) of f where f_x = f_y = 0, discarding any where a partial derivative does not exist; calculate the discriminant D = f_xx f_yy − (f_xy)² at each; and apply the second derivative test to decide whether each is a local maximum, local minimum or saddle point, or whether the test is inconclusive.

concepts.name: Bounded set
concepts.statement: A set is bounded if all the points in that set can be contained within a ball (or disk) of finite radius; a closed, bounded set replaces the closed interval of one variable.

concepts.name: Extreme value theorem for functions of two variables
concepts.statement: A continuous function f(x, y) on a closed and bounded set D in the plane attains an absolute maximum value at some point of D and an absolute minimum value at some point of D.

concepts.name: Finding extreme values of a function of two variables
concepts.statement: If z = f(x, y) is differentiable on a closed, bounded set D, its absolute maximum and minimum values are the largest and smallest values found among the values of f at the critical points of f in D and the values of f on the boundary of D; it follows from the extreme value theorem and Fermat's theorem.

concepts.name: Finding absolute maximum and minimum values
concepts.statement: To find the absolute extrema of a continuous, differentiable f on a closed, bounded set D: determine the critical points of f in D, calculate f at each, determine the maximum and minimum values of f on the boundary (parameterizing its segments or curves, or by Lagrange multipliers), and take the largest and smallest of all these values.

concepts.name: Constraint
concepts.statement: A constraint is an inequality or equation involving one or more variables that is used in an optimization problem; it enforces a limit on the possible solutions, such as the budget 20x + 4y ≤ 216 on golf balls and advertising.

concepts.name: Objective function
concepts.statement: In an optimization problem, the objective function is the function f(x, y) that is to be maximized or minimized subject to the constraints.

concepts.name: Method of Lagrange multipliers: one constraint
concepts.statement: Let f and g be functions of two variables with continuous partial derivatives at every point of some open set containing the smooth curve g(x, y) = 0. If f, restricted to points on the curve g(x, y) = 0, has a local extremum at (x₀, y₀) and ∇g(x₀, y₀) ≠ 0, then there is a number λ, called a Lagrange multiplier, for which ∇f(x₀, y₀) = λ∇g(x₀, y₀): at the extremum the level curve of f is tangent to the constraint and the two gradients are parallel. With three variables the same equations ∇f = λ∇g, g = 0 are solved.

concepts.name: Lagrange multiplier
concepts.statement: A Lagrange multiplier is the constant (or constants) used in the method of Lagrange multipliers; in the case of one constant, it is represented by the variable λ.

concepts.name: Steps for using Lagrange multipliers
concepts.statement: Determine the objective function f(x, y) and the constraint function g(x, y), and whether f is to be maximized or minimized; set up the system ∇f(x₀, y₀) = λ∇g(x₀, y₀), g(x₀, y₀) = 0; solve for x₀ and y₀; the largest of the values of f at the solutions maximizes f and the smallest minimizes it.

concepts.name: Lagrange multipliers with two constraints
concepts.statement: To optimize w = f(x, y, z) subject to two constraints g(x, y, z) = 0 and h(x, y, z) = 0, there are two Lagrange multipliers λ₁ and λ₂, and the system of equations is ∇f(x₀, y₀, z₀) = λ₁∇g(x₀, y₀, z₀) + λ₂∇h(x₀, y₀, z₀), g(x₀, y₀, z₀) = 0, h(x₀, y₀, z₀) = 0.
